Copy the entry below, paste the copy directly under this block, and edit it.
Newest post first — the page renders these in file order.
id           unique slug, lower-case-with-dashes. An entry without one is ignored.
image        "/journal/my-post.jpg" for a file in public/journal/, or a full

excerpt      1-2 sentence summary of the LinkedIn post.

imageAlt: Two identical white capsules side by side. The card beneath the left one reads "clinically dosed, bioavailable, evidence-backed" with a tick; the card beneath the right reads "real ingredient, wrong dose, wrong form" with a cross.
title: The placebo problem: what an under-dosed formula cannot outperform
excerpt: A new study found real improvements in memory, physical performance and stress from placebo pills — even when people knew the pills were fake. Most supplements are dosed too low to clear that baseline.

imageAlt: Typographic card reading "Clinically proven. The two most abused words in the supplement industry."
title: Call the formulator before you call the manufacturer
excerpt: A manufacturer will quote and build exactly what you hand them — including a formula whose hero ingredient isn't TGA-permitted, or whose dose doesn't match the evidence you plan to cite. Formulating first is what makes everything downstream straightforward.

imageAlt: Carousel cover reading "The truth behind clinically proven on supplement labels", with a cracked flask and a mortar both labelled "clinically proven", a 50mg ingredient tag struck through, and questions asking about dose matching, which studies, what population and real results.
title: What "clinically proven" actually proves
excerpt: An ingredient can be studied at 600mg and included in a product at 50mg — the claim still stands, the efficacy almost certainly doesn't. Under the TGA's listed medicine framework, permitted indications must be substantiated, but nothing forces the dose on the label to match the dose in the literature.

imageAlt: A marble bench laid with two bowls of white powder labelled magnesium oxide and magnesium glycinate, a bowl of turmeric beside fresh root, two capsules and a black Formulyn dropper bottle. An open notebook headed "bioavailability ≠ digestion" sets methylcobalamin against cyanocobalamin and closes with "not all forms are created equal".
title: Bioavailability is not digestion
excerpt: Magnesium oxide absorbs at rates as low as 4%; B12 as cyanocobalamin needs a conversion some people cannot efficiently make. Same mineral, same vitamin on the label — the form, the delivery system and the excipient matrix decide whether any of it reaches the bloodstream.
